before.exam_tip_html: In the AQA English Literature exam, Animal Farm questions always ask you to write about both what happens in the text and how Orwell presents ideas. Context is not a bolt-on — embed it within your analysis of language, form and structure. When you identify a literary technique (allegory, satire, irony), always explain why Orwell uses it and what political message it conveys. For 34-mark essay questions, SPaG marks are awarded for accurate spelling, punctuation and use of specialist vocabulary like ‘allegory’, ‘totalitarianism’ and ‘propaganda’.
before.content_html:
What Kind of Story Is Animal Farm?

Animal Farm is not simply a story about animals on a farm. Orwell deliberately chose the form of a fable — a short story with animal characters that teaches a moral lesson. By giving human qualities to animals (a technique called anthropomorphism), Orwell made complex political ideas accessible and memorable. The subtitle ‘A Fairy Story’ is deliberately ironic: the content is anything but light-hearted.

Key Fact

Orwell subtitled Animal Farm ‘A Fairy Story’ as an ironic joke. The novella is actually a dark political warning about how power corrupts revolutionary ideals.

Fables have existed for thousands of years. The ancient Greek storyteller Aesop wrote fables like ‘The Hare and the Tortoise’ and ‘The Lion and the Mouse’, each containing a moral message delivered through animal characters. Orwell follows this tradition but takes it much further, using the form to deliver a sustained political argument.

Allegory: The Hidden Meaning

Animal Farm is an allegory — a story where characters, events and settings represent real-world people and situations. Almost every element of the novella maps onto the history of the Russian Revolution and Soviet Union under Stalin. Understanding these connections is essential for the exam.

Mr Jones represents Tsar Nicholas II, the incompetent ruler whose neglect triggered revolution. Old Major represents Karl Marx (the political theorist) and Vladimir Lenin (the revolutionary leader). Napoleon represents Joseph Stalin, the dictator who seized power through fear and violence. Snowball represents Leon Trotsky, the intellectual rival whom Stalin exiled and eventually had murdered. Squealer represents Soviet propaganda, particularly the state newspaper Pravda (meaning ‘truth’). Boxer represents the loyal, exploited working class.

Satire: Humour with a Serious Purpose

Orwell also uses satire throughout Animal Farm. Satire uses humour, exaggeration and irony to mock and criticise. When the pigs start sleeping in beds and then change the commandment to ‘No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets’, the dark comedy exposes how those in power twist rules to suit themselves. The humour makes the political message more powerful because it highlights the absurdity of totalitarianism.

The Russian Revolution: Essential Context

Before 1917, Russia was ruled by Tsar Nicholas II, who had total control over a country where most people lived in extreme poverty. Anger over poverty, lack of political freedom, and Russia’s failures in World War I led to two revolutions in 1917. In February, protests forced the Tsar to abdicate. In October, the Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, seized power. They were inspired by the ideas of Karl Marx, who argued that the working class (the proletariat) should overthrow the ruling class and share wealth equally.

Key Fact

After Lenin’s death in 1924, Joseph Stalin took control of the Soviet Union. He ruled through fear, propaganda, purges and a cult of personality — exactly the pattern Orwell mirrors through Napoleon in Animal Farm.

George Orwell (born Eric Arthur Blair, 1903) was a democratic socialist who believed in equality and freedom. His experience fighting in the Spanish Civil War (1936) was pivotal: he witnessed Soviet-backed communists attacking their own allies, showing him that revolutionary ideals could be betrayed by those seeking power. After Spain, Orwell became fiercely opposed to totalitarianism in all its forms. He wrote Animal Farm in 1945 specifically to show how Stalin had corrupted the ideals of the Russian Revolution. Crucially, Orwell was not attacking socialism itself — he was attacking its corruption under authoritarian rule.

Why Does This Context Matter in the Exam?

You are expected to weave contextual knowledge throughout your essays, not bolt it on as a separate paragraph. When you analyse a quotation, connect it to what you know about the Russian Revolution, Orwell’s beliefs, or the literary form. For example, when discussing Napoleon’s use of the dogs, link this to Stalin’s secret police (the NKVD). When analysing Squealer’s speeches, connect them to Pravda and Soviet propaganda. This shows you understand Orwell’s purpose.

Key Fact

A common misconception is that Orwell was attacking communism itself. In fact, he was a democratic socialist who criticised how revolutionary ideals were betrayed under Stalin’s totalitarian regime.

before.content_html:
Life After the Rebellion

Chapter 3 opens with the animals working harder than ever — but, crucially, working for themselves. Orwell writes that they ‘toiled and sweated’ to bring in the harvest, yet the mood is optimistic. The farm is productive and the animals feel a sense of ownership. This brief period represents the early promise of the revolution, before corruption takes hold. However, Orwell immediately begins planting clues that this utopia will not last.

From the very start of Chapter 3, inequality is visible. The pigs ‘did not actually work, but directed and supervised the others.’ Orwell uses this parenthetical observation to show how intellectual superiority is being used to justify a new class system. The pigs position themselves as ‘brainworkers’ whose management is essential, while animals like Boxer do all the physical labour. This mirrors how the Bolshevik leadership claimed special privileges because their intellectual work was vital to the state.

Key Fact

The pigs never do any physical work on the farm. Their role as organisers and supervisors mirrors the communist party officials who lived in luxury while ordinary Soviet citizens laboured in poverty.

Boxer: The Loyal Worker

Boxer the carthorse emerges in Chapter 3 as the most dedicated worker on the farm. His personal motto — ‘I will work harder’ — captures his absolute devotion to the cause. Orwell presents Boxer as both admirable and deeply vulnerable: his strength and loyalty are exploited by the pigs, who benefit from his labour without ever rewarding it. Boxer represents the proletariat — the loyal, hardworking ordinary people who are most exploited under totalitarian regimes.

Benjamin the donkey provides a contrasting perspective. His cynical remark — ‘Donkeys live a long time. None of you has ever seen a dead donkey’ — suggests he knows the revolution will not deliver on its promises. Benjamin represents those who see through political lies but do nothing to resist, making his silence a form of complicity.

Orwell uses the animals’ varying ability to read as a metaphor for education and power. The pigs read fluently, giving them exclusive access to written rules. The dogs can read but show no interest. Boxer learns only four letters of the alphabet. The sheep can manage nothing more than the simplified slogan ‘Four legs good, two legs bad.’ This reduction of the Seven Commandments to a single slogan demonstrates how propaganda works: complex ideas are simplified until they become meaningless chants that can be used to shut down debate.

The Milk and Apples: Squealer’s First Manipulation

The milk that disappeared at the end of Chapter 2 is now mixed into the pigs’ mash. The windfall apples are also reserved exclusively for the pigs. When the other animals question this, Squealer is sent to explain. His speech in Chapter 3 is the first major example of manipulation through language — and it establishes the template for how the pigs will control the farm throughout the novella.

Squealer’s defence follows a clear pattern. First, he appeals to ethos: ‘You do not imagine, I hope, that we pigs are doing this in a spirit of selfishness and privilege?’ The rhetorical question is structured to make disagreement seem unreasonable. Then he appeals to logos: ‘Milk and apples (this has been proved by Science, comrades) contain substances absolutely necessary to the well-being of a pig.’ The parenthetical ‘this has been proved by Science’ is a false appeal to authority — Squealer presents an unverifiable claim as established fact.

Key Fact

Squealer’s most powerful weapon is fear. His speech always returns to the same threat: ‘Jones would come back!’ This is a scapegoat tactic — by invoking the threat of the old regime, Squealer makes the animals accept any injustice as preferable to the return of Jones.

Squealer employs several propaganda techniques in this speech. Fear: ‘Jones would come back! Yes, Jones would come back!’ — the repetition intensifies the threat. False statistics: the claim that science proves pigs need apples is unverifiable. Euphemism: calling self-interest ‘preserving our health’. Appeal to authority: positioning the pigs as essential ‘brainworkers’. Emotional blackmail: ‘It is for your sake that we drink that milk’ — the italics on ‘your’ invert the truth, making the pigs’ greed seem like self-sacrifice. Orwell notes that ‘it was agreed without further argument’ — the passive voice again hides who agreed, suggesting the animals are already losing their ability to challenge authority.

Squealer as Pravda

Squealer represents the Soviet state media, particularly the newspaper Pravda (meaning ‘truth’). Just as Pravda presented Stalin’s policies as beneficial and necessary, Squealer reframes the pigs’ greed as self-sacrifice for the common good. The irony is devastating: the character whose name suggests high-pitched noise and complaint is the one who silences all complaint. When Orwell describes him as being able to ‘turn black into white’, he captures the essence of propaganda — making the population believe the opposite of what is true.

Key Fact

By Chapter 3, Orwell has established the three pillars of the pigs’ control: intellectual superiority (the pigs as ‘brainworkers’), propaganda (Squealer’s speeches), and fear (‘Jones would come back’). These mirror Stalin’s use of the party elite, state media, and the threat of counter-revolution.

lessons.title: The Battle of the Cowshed & Snowball's Leadership

before.content_html:
The Battle of the Cowshed

Chapter 4 marks a turning point in Animal Farm. News of the rebellion has spread to neighbouring farms — Foxwood (run by the easygoing Mr Pilkington) and Pinchfield (run by the tough, shrewd Mr Frederick). Jones, with the help of men from both farms, launches an attack to reclaim Manor Farm. The Battle of the Cowshed is Animal Farm’s equivalent of the Russian Civil War (1918–1921), in which forces loyal to the Tsar (the ‘Whites’) tried to overthrow the Bolsheviks (the ‘Reds’).

Orwell uses the battle to contrast two styles of leadership. Snowball has studied Julius Caesar’s military campaigns and devised a tactical defence. He leads from the front, personally charging at Jones and being wounded by shotgun pellets. Napoleon, by contrast, is entirely absent from the action. This distinction matters greatly: in the allegory, Snowball represents Leon Trotsky, who commanded the Red Army and was instrumental in winning the Civil War, while Napoleon represents Stalin, who contributed little militarily but later claimed credit.

Key Fact

Snowball represents Leon Trotsky, commander of the Red Army. His bravery at the Battle of the Cowshed parallels Trotsky’s crucial role in winning the Russian Civil War. Napoleon’s absence mirrors Stalin’s limited military contribution.

Snowball’s Leadership Qualities

Orwell presents Snowball as an energetic, intelligent and genuinely committed leader. He is described charging ‘straight for Jones’ — the directness of the language reflects his courage. When he is hit by shotgun pellets, the wound becomes a badge of honour rather than a deterrent. Snowball is creative (he designs the windmill plans), idealistic (he wants to improve the animals’ lives through education and technology) and eloquent (‘Snowball often won over the majority by his brilliant speeches’).

However, Orwell does not present Snowball as entirely heroic. He too benefits from the pigs’ privileges and uses the slogan ‘Four legs good, two legs bad’ to simplify debate. A common exam misconception is to treat Snowball as wholly good and Napoleon as wholly evil. Orwell’s characterisation is more nuanced: both pigs participate in the early corruption, but their methods of leadership differ dramatically.

Snowball leads through persuasion, debate and intellectual argument. He is a ‘persuasive speaker’ and a ‘strategic thinker’ who cares about education and promotes open discussion. Napoleon operates differently: he is ‘better at canvassing support for himself in between times’ — working behind the scenes rather than in public debate. Napoleon uses authority and fear rather than argument. His secret rearing of the dogs (taking the puppies away ‘to educate them himself’) is the most sinister act of the early chapters — he is building a private army while Snowball focuses on improving the farm.

Motif: Rituals and Ceremony

After the battle, Orwell introduces the motif of rituals and ceremonies. The animals create military decorations: ‘Animal Hero, First Class’ (awarded to Snowball and Boxer) and ‘Animal Hero, Second Class’ (awarded posthumously to the dead sheep). They also establish a ritual of firing Jones’s gun twice a year — on the anniversary of the Battle of the Cowshed and on Midsummer Day. These rituals serve a dual purpose.

On one level, rituals create a sense of belonging, pride and shared identity. They commemorate sacrifice and reinforce the animals’ commitment to the revolution. On another level, rituals are tools of control. They create emotional attachment to the regime, making it harder for animals to question authority. Orwell shows how totalitarian governments use ceremonies, medals and parades to generate loyalty — just as Stalin used Victory Day celebrations and military parades to strengthen his cult of personality.

Key Fact

The Battle of the Cowshed is later rewritten by the pigs. Napoleon claims credit for the victory and accuses Snowball of being a traitor who fought on Jones’s side. This rewriting of history is one of Orwell’s most important themes — it mirrors how Stalin erased Trotsky from Soviet history.

The Neighbouring Farms

Foxwood and Pinchfield represent the Western capitalist powers. Mr Pilkington (Foxwood) is easygoing and neglectful, representing Britain. Mr Frederick (Pinchfield) is tough and shrewd, representing Germany. Their initial hostility to Animal Farm mirrors Western opposition to the Soviet Union. The fact that they spread rumours about the farm — ‘the animals practised tyranny against their own kind’ — while simultaneously fearing the revolution could spread, reflects the complex relationship between the Western world and the USSR during the Cold War.

The battle is crucial to the novella’s structure for three reasons. First, it establishes Snowball as a genuine hero, making his later expulsion more shocking and unjust. Second, it provides raw material for the pigs’ propaganda — the battle is progressively rewritten until Snowball is remembered as a villain and Napoleon as the saviour. Third, it creates the rituals (gun-firing, medals) that the pigs later use to consolidate emotional control over the animals. Every element of this chapter is repurposed by Napoleon’s regime to serve its own interests.

Key Fact

Boxer shows both his strength and his moral sensitivity during the battle. After striking a stable-lad who appears dead, Boxer exclaims ‘I have no wish to take life, not even human life.’ This compassion contrasts sharply with Napoleon’s later willingness to execute animals without remorse.

before.content_html:
The Power Struggle

Chapter 5 is the turning point of Animal Farm. The tension between Snowball and Napoleon that has been building since the rebellion finally erupts. Orwell presents the two pigs as fundamentally opposed: Snowball wants to build a windmill to improve the animals’ lives through technology and reduced labour, while Napoleon dismisses the plan and argues that food production should be the priority. Their disagreement is not really about windmills — it is about the kind of society Animal Farm will become.

Orwell makes the allegorical parallel explicit. Snowball, representing Trotsky, believes in spreading the revolution and improving conditions through innovation. Napoleon, representing Stalin, is focused on consolidating his own power. In the Soviet Union, Trotsky advocated ‘permanent revolution’ (exporting communism worldwide), while Stalin pushed ‘socialism in one country’ (strengthening the USSR internally). The windmill debate mirrors this real ideological conflict.

Key Fact

The windmill debate represents the real power struggle between Trotsky and Stalin after Lenin’s death. Orwell shows that Napoleon never cared about the windmill itself — he opposed it only because Snowball supported it, then claimed it as his own idea after expelling Snowball.

Mollie’s Departure

Before the climactic expulsion, Orwell includes the departure of Mollie, the vain white mare who loves sugar lumps and ribbons. Mollie represents the bourgeoisie — those who benefited from the old system and have no interest in revolutionary ideals. She is described from Chapter 1 as ‘foolish’ and materialistic, more concerned with ribbons and sugar than with freedom. Her defection to a human owner shows that some members of society will always prioritise personal comfort over collective justice.

Orwell’s presentation of Mollie is deliberately unsympathetic, but it also raises a genuine question: can people be blamed for leaving a revolution that increasingly demands sacrifice without delivering its promises? Mollie departs just before Napoleon seizes absolute power — ironically, she escapes the worst of the totalitarian regime that follows.

Snowball’s Expulsion

The expulsion of Snowball is the most dramatic moment in the novella so far. During a debate about the windmill, just as Snowball is winning the argument with ‘his brilliant speeches’, Napoleon lets out a ‘high-pitched whimper’ and nine enormous dogs — the puppies he secretly reared — burst into the barn and chase Snowball from the farm. The animals are terrified. The dogs, described as ‘huge’ and ‘fierce-looking’, represent Stalin’s secret police (the NKVD), who enforced his rule through intimidation, imprisonment and execution.

Key Fact

The nine dogs represent Stalin’s NKVD (secret police). Napoleon’s ‘high-pitched whimper’ is a deliberate signal — he has been planning this coup from the moment he took the puppies away to ‘educate’ them. Force, not argument, is how he seizes power.

The expulsion parallels Trotsky’s exile from the Soviet Union in 1929. Just as Stalin used the apparatus of the state to remove his rival, Napoleon uses the dogs to remove his. Crucially, Napoleon does not defeat Snowball in argument — he defeats him through violence. Orwell’s message is clear: in a totalitarian system, reasoned debate is no match for brute force.

After Snowball’s expulsion, Napoleon moves swiftly to consolidate absolute power. He cancels the Sunday meetings where animals debated policy, replacing democratic discussion with a committee of pigs who make all decisions. He sits on a raised platform with the dogs arranged around him — a visual symbol of hierarchy and intimidation. He then announces that the windmill will be built after all, claiming it was his idea all along. Squealer explains that Napoleon only appeared to oppose the windmill as ‘tactics’ — rewriting recent history that the animals witnessed with their own eyes.

Squealer’s Role

Squealer’s propaganda reaches a new level in Chapter 5. He tells the animals that Snowball was ‘always a traitor’ and that Napoleon had to protect them. When Boxer objects, saying ‘He fought bravely at the Battle of the Cowshed’, Squealer responds that ‘loyalty and obedience are more important’ than bravery. This is a chilling moment: Squealer is teaching the animals that loyalty to Napoleon matters more than truth. The narrator notes that ‘the three dogs who happened to be with [Squealer] growled so threateningly’ that Boxer falls silent. Propaganda backed by violence — this is the formula of totalitarian control.

After seizing power, Napoleon places Old Major’s skull on display, requiring the animals to file past it every Sunday. This transforms a revolutionary thinker into a religious-like icon. It parallels Stalin’s treatment of Lenin’s body, which was embalmed and placed in a mausoleum in Red Square for public veneration. In both cases, the original leader’s ideas are hollowed out and turned into a tool of cult of personality. Napoleon claims to continue Old Major’s legacy while doing the exact opposite of what Old Major taught.

Key Fact

After Snowball’s expulsion, Boxer adopts a second motto: ‘Napoleon is always right.’ Combined with ‘I will work harder’, these two maxims capture the tragedy of the working class under totalitarianism — unquestioning loyalty to a leader who will ultimately betray them.

before.content_html:
Building the Windmill

After Snowball’s expulsion, Napoleon announces that the windmill will be built after all — despite having opposed it. Scapegoating Snowball allows Napoleon to claim the windmill idea as his own, rewriting history to maintain power. Squealer explains that Napoleon had never really opposed the windmill but had pretended to in order to get rid of Snowball — a masterpiece of propaganda.

The animals work gruelling sixty-hour weeks. Orwell writes that ‘all that year the animals worked like slaves’ — a deeply ironic simile, since the entire purpose of the Rebellion was to free them from slavery. The windmill becomes a symbol of the animals’ exploited labour: they sacrifice everything for a project that benefits only the pigs.

Key Fact

The windmill represents Stalin’s Five-Year Plans — ambitious industrial projects that demanded backbreaking labour from Soviet workers, often with little reward. Orwell uses the windmill to show how leaders exploit workers’ hope for a better future.

Boxer: The Hero Worker

Boxer is the driving force behind the windmill. Orwell writes that ‘nothing could have been achieved’ without him and that his strength was ‘equal to that of all the rest of the animals put together.’ The vivid image of ‘the tips of his hoofs clawing at the ground’ conveys extreme physical effort, suggesting someone at the very edge of their endurance.

Boxer adopts the personal motto ‘Napoleon is always right’ alongside his original ‘I will work harder.’ This combination of blind loyalty and relentless labour makes Boxer both admirable and tragic. He represents the proletariat — the working class who pour everything into the system but are ultimately betrayed by those in power.

Boxer parallels Alexei Stakhanov, a Soviet coal miner who in 1935 produced fourteen times his daily target in a single shift. Stalin used Stakhanov as propaganda — a poster boy for the idea that hard work brought happiness. The ‘Stakhanovite movement’ pressured workers across the USSR to exceed targets, just as Boxer’s example inspires the other animals to work harder.

Like Boxer, Stakhanov was rewarded with praise and small comforts but was ultimately discarded. After Stalin’s death, Stakhanov was sent back to the mines and spent his final years in obscurity, drinking heavily. Orwell uses Boxer to warn that totalitarian regimes exploit loyal workers and discard them when they are no longer useful.

The Changing Commandments

In Chapter Six, the pigs move into the farmhouse and begin sleeping in beds — a direct violation of the Fourth Commandment. When Clover checks the barn wall, the commandment now reads: ‘No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets.’ Orwell writes that ‘curiously enough, Clover had not remembered that the Fourth Commandment mentioned sheets.’ This dramatic irony highlights the animals’ inability to challenge the pigs’ lies.

Squealer justifies every change by arguing that the pigs need comfort to do their ‘brainwork.’ He is always ‘attended by two or three dogs’ — a subtle reminder that propaganda is backed by the threat of violence. The gradual alteration of the commandments is one of Orwell’s most powerful devices: it shows how totalitarian regimes change the rules bit by bit, so slowly that people fail to notice until it is too late.

Key Fact

Each commandment change mirrors a real betrayal of communist ideals under Stalin. The beds represent luxury; trading with humans mirrors the USSR’s alliances with capitalist nations. Orwell shows that revolutionary principles are always the first casualty of power.

Engagement with Humans

Napoleon hires Mr Whymper as a solicitor to handle trade with neighbouring farms. This directly contradicts the original principles of Animalism, which forbade all contact with humans. Squealer insists the arrangement is ‘not of course for any commercial purpose’ — a laughable euphemism that Orwell uses to expose the gap between the pigs’ words and their actions.

When a storm destroys the windmill, Napoleon immediately blames Snowball, declaring that he acted ‘in sheer malignity, thinking to set back our plans.’ Most animals accept this explanation without question — only Boxer hesitates. Napoleon uses the destruction to intensify hatred of Snowball and to rally the animals to rebuild, extracting even more labour from them. This parallels how Stalin blamed economic failures on Trotsky and ‘saboteurs’ rather than admitting flaws in his own Five-Year Plans.

before.content_html:
The Purges Begin

Chapter Seven marks the darkest turning point in Animal Farm. Facing food shortages and growing unrest, Napoleon responds not with reform but with terror. He summons all the animals to the yard and, with his dogs at his side, forces a series of confessions. The four pigs who had protested against Napoleon’s abolition of Sunday meetings are the first to confess to conspiring with Snowball. The dogs ‘promptly tore their throats out.’

This triggers a cascade of confessions. Hens, geese, and sheep all come forward to admit to various crimes — stealing corn, urinating in the drinking pool, killing an old ram. Each confession is followed by immediate execution. Orwell writes that ‘the air was heavy with the smell of blood, which had been unknown there since Jones was expelled.’ The sensory language creates an overwhelming atmosphere of horror, and the reference to Jones is devastating: the revolution has produced something just as brutal as what it replaced.

Key Fact

The purges in Chapter Seven directly parallel Stalin’s Great Purge (1936–1938), during which millions of Soviet citizens were imprisoned, forced to confess to fabricated crimes, and executed. Public ‘show trials’ were staged to create the illusion that Stalin was protecting the nation from internal enemies.

The Language of Brutality

Orwell uses visceral, violent language to convey the horror of the executions. The dogs ‘seized four of the pigs by the ear’ and the victims came forward ‘trembling, with guilt written on every line of their countenances.’ The pigs are described as ‘squealing with pain and terror’ — a word choice that reduces them to their animal nature and strips them of dignity.

The phrase ‘the dogs had tasted blood, and for a few moments they appeared to go quite mad’ is particularly chilling. The personification of the dogs as blood-crazed killers mirrors the behaviour of the NKVD, Stalin’s secret police, who carried out executions with increasing brutality. ‘A pile of corpses lying before Napoleon’s feet’ creates a stark visual image of Napoleon as a tyrant surveying his victims.

Stalin launched the Great Purge because he was deeply paranoid about losing control. He blamed economic failures — particularly the disastrous results of his Five-Year Plans — on ‘saboteurs’ and ‘enemies of the people.’ The NKVD (secret police) arrested thousands, extracting forced confessions through torture and the threat of death.

Nikolai Yezhov, head of the NKVD from 1936 to 1938, organised mass arrests and executions on Stalin’s orders. After serving his purpose, Yezhov himself was arrested and executed in 1940 — then erased from official photographs. This ‘rewriting of history’ directly parallels the pigs’ constant revision of events on Animal Farm.

Scapegoating Snowball

Squealer’s propaganda reaches its most manipulative in Chapter Seven. He announces that Snowball ‘has sold himself to Frederick of Pinchfield Farm’ and was ‘in league with Jones from the very start.’ This scapegoating rewrites history entirely — the animals saw Snowball fight bravely at the Battle of the Cowshed, yet Squealer insists that was ‘part of the arrangement.’

Even Boxer questions this: ‘I do not believe that. Snowball fought bravely at the Battle of the Cowshed. I saw him myself.’ But Squealer counters by invoking Napoleon’s absolute authority: ‘Our Leader, Comrade Napoleon, has stated categorically — categorically, comrade — that Snowball was Jones’s agent from the very beginning.’ Boxer’s response — ‘If Comrade Napoleon says it, it must be right’ — is devastating. It shows how even the most loyal and well-meaning animals can be manipulated into accepting obvious lies.

Key Fact

Squealer’s speech uses multiple propaganda techniques: fear (‘Snowball’s secret agents are lurking among us’), scapegoating (blaming Snowball for all problems), appeal to authority (‘Comrade Napoleon has stated categorically’), and loaded language (‘in sheer malignity’). These parallel techniques used by Soviet newspaper Pravda under Stalin.

Banning ‘Beasts of England’

After the executions, the surviving animals huddle together in shock. Clover looks out over the farm and reflects that ‘these scenes of terror and slaughter were not what they had looked forward to on that night when Old Major first stirred them to rebellion.’ This moment of clarity is heartbreaking — but also futile. Clover cannot articulate her thoughts and lacks the words to challenge the pigs.

The animals begin singing ‘Beasts of England’ — the revolutionary anthem that once inspired their dreams of freedom. Squealer announces that the song is now banned. His justification is that ‘the Rebellion is now completed’ and the song is ‘no longer needed.’ In reality, the song is dangerous because it reminds the animals of the revolution’s original promises — promises that Napoleon has comprehensively broken.

The replacement anthem, composed by Minimus, is a hollow piece of propaganda praising ‘Animal Farm, Animal Farm, never through me shalt thou come to harm.’ Where ‘Beasts of England’ was about liberation, the new song is about obedience. Orwell shows how totalitarian regimes suppress symbols of resistance and replace them with state-approved alternatives.

Napoleon’s Cult of Personality

By Chapter Eight, Napoleon has transformed from a political leader into a figure of worship. He is no longer referred to simply as ‘Napoleon’ but as ‘our Leader, Comrade Napoleon.’ The pigs invent grandiose titles for him: ‘Father of All Animals, Terror of Mankind, Protector of the Sheep-fold, Ducklings’ Friend.’ These epithets are absurdly contradictory — he cannot be both ‘Terror of Mankind’ and ‘Ducklings’ Friend’ — and Orwell uses this to satirise how dictators construct false images of themselves.

Napoleon now rarely appears in public. When he does, he is ‘attended not only by his retinue of dogs but by a black cockerel who marched in front of him and acted as a kind of trumpeter.’ He eats alone from the ‘Crown Derby dinner service’ and has a gun fired on his birthday. Orwell builds a picture of a leader who has isolated himself from ordinary life — exactly the opposite of Old Major’s vision of equality.

Key Fact

A cult of personality is a common feature of totalitarian regimes. Napoleon’s cult parallels Stalin’s: portraits of Stalin were displayed in every Soviet building, cities were named after him, and he was credited with every national achievement.

Minimus’s Poem — Propaganda as Art

The pig Minimus composes a poem entitled ‘Comrade Napoleon,’ which begins: ‘Friend of fatherless! Fountain of happiness! Lord of the swill-bucket!’ The poem uses religious language (‘Thou art the giver of all that thy creatures love’) and deification to elevate Napoleon to an almost god-like status. The line ‘His first squeak should be “Comrade Napoleon!”’ suggests that loyalty to the leader should begin from birth.

Orwell’s satire is sharp here. The phrase ‘Lord of the swill-bucket’ is deliberately bathetic — it deflates the grand, religious tone by reminding us that Napoleon is, after all, a pig eating from a trough. The poem is inscribed on the barn wall opposite the Seven Commandments, with a portrait of Napoleon painted by Squealer. This visual juxtaposition is powerful: Napoleon’s image is literally placed above the rules that he has systematically broken.

Stalin’s cult of personality involved portraits in every home, statues in every city, and mandatory praise in all public speeches. Propaganda posters depicted him as a kindly father figure — ‘Father of Nations’ — while he oversaw mass starvation and political murder. Similar cults were built around Mao Zedong in China, Kim Il-sung in North Korea, and Adolf Hitler in Nazi Germany. In each case, the leader used propaganda, art, and ritual to make themselves appear infallible and all-powerful.

Orwell understood that a cult of personality serves a specific purpose: it makes criticism of the leader feel like blasphemy. When Napoleon is presented as ‘Father of All Animals,’ questioning him becomes an attack on everyone’s father. This is why the animals give Napoleon credit for everything — even a hen remarks that ‘under the guidance of our Leader, Comrade Napoleon, I have laid five eggs in six days.’

The Battle of the Windmill

In Chapter Eight, Napoleon sells a stack of timber to Mr Frederick of Pinchfield Farm, only to discover that Frederick has paid with forged banknotes. Frederick then attacks Animal Farm with armed men who blow up the completed windmill with blasting powder. Orwell writes that ‘a mighty cry of vengeance went up’ from the animals, who fight back ferociously and eventually drive Frederick’s men off the farm.

The destruction of the windmill — the product of years of backbreaking labour — is a devastating blow. Yet Napoleon immediately declares it a glorious victory: the ‘Battle of the Windmill.’ He creates a new decoration, the ‘Order of the Green Banner,’ which he awards to himself. Two days of celebrations follow. This is a masterclass in spin: turning a catastrophic failure into a propaganda triumph.

Key Fact

Frederick’s betrayal and attack parallel Hitler’s betrayal of the Nazi-Soviet Pact in 1941, when Germany invaded the Soviet Union despite their non-aggression treaty. Stalin, like Napoleon, had been deceived — and reframed the devastating early defeats as heroic Soviet resistance.

Orwell’s Irony: The Pigs and Whisky

After the battle celebrations, the pigs discover a case of whisky in the farmhouse cellar. That night, ‘the sound of loud singing’ comes from the farmhouse, and Napoleon is ‘distinctly seen to emerge from the back door, gallop rapidly round the yard, and disappear indoors again’ — wearing Mr Jones’s old bowler hat. The image of a pig drunkenly galloping in a human hat is both comic and deeply ironic: Napoleon is literally becoming the human tyrant he replaced.

The morning after the drinking, Squealer announces that Napoleon is dying. A ‘cry of lamentation went up’ and the animals walk on tiptoe around the farmhouse. Napoleon’s ‘last act upon earth’ is to decree that drinking alcohol shall be punished by death. Of course, Napoleon is simply hungover. The Fifth Commandment is later changed to ‘No animal shall drink alcohol to excess’ — another incremental erosion of the original principles. Orwell’s irony here is exquisite: the pigs break a rule, then simply rewrite it to excuse their behaviour.

practice_questions.text: Read the following quotation: 'Father of All Animals, Terror of Mankind, Protector of the Sheep-fold, Ducklings' Friend.' How does Orwell use language to satirise Napoleon's cult of personality?
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of language choices. E.g. The epithets are deliberately contradictory — 'Terror of Mankind' suggests fear and power, while 'Ducklings' Friend' suggests warmth and gentleness. The juxtaposition is absurd, and Orwell uses this absurdity to satirise how dictators construct a false, all-encompassing image. 'Father of All Animals' echoes Stalin's title 'Father of Nations', explicitly linking Napoleon to the Soviet dictator. The accumulation of titles mimics the excessive praise typical of totalitarian propaganda.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comments. E.g. Napoleon has lots of different titles which makes him seem important.

practice_questions.text: Starting with the extract describing the poem 'Comrade Napoleon' ('Friend of fatherless! Fountain of happiness! Lord of the swill-bucket!'), explore how Orwell uses language to present propaganda in Animal Farm. Write about: how Orwell presents propaganda in this extract, and how Orwell presents propaganda in the novel as a whole.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. The poem uses religious register ('Thou art the giver') to deify Napoleon, making criticism feel like blasphemy. 'Lord of the swill-bucket' is bathetic — the grand religious language collapses into the mundane reality of pig-food, exposing the absurdity. 'His first squeak should be Comrade Napoleon' suggests totalitarian indoctrination from birth. The poem is inscribed opposite the Seven Commandments — Napoleon's image literally replaces the revolution's principles. Across the novel, propaganda evolves from Squealer's verbal arguments to this kind of cultural saturation. Context: parallels Pravda, Soviet art, and mandatory praise of Stalin.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear, relevant analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Orwell use the character of Napoleon to explore ideas about power and control in Animal Farm? Write about: how Orwell presents the character of Napoleon, and how Orwell uses the character of Napoleon to present ideas about power and control in the novel.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26–30 marks + up to 4 spelling/grammar)Critical, exploratory response. Napoleon's rise to power follows a clear trajectory: political manoeuvring (using the dogs to exile Snowball), consolidation through fear (the purges of Chapter Seven), and the creation of a cult of personality (Chapter Eight). Orwell shows that power corrupts absolutely — Napoleon begins as one pig among many and ends as an indistinguishable copy of Jones. His epithets ('Father of All Animals') parallel Stalin's self-glorification. The cult of personality makes him untouchable: criticism becomes impossible when the leader is presented as infallible. Napoleon's methods — propaganda (Squealer), violence (the dogs), and manipulation of history (changing the commandments) — are the three pillars of totalitarian control. The Battle of the Windmill shows his ability to turn failure into propaganda victory. The whisky episode reveals his hypocrisy: he punishes others for what he does himself. Context: Napoleon represents Stalin, but also any leader who uses power for self-enrichment rather than the public good.

practice_questions.text: Starting with the extract describing the Battle of the Windmill and its aftermath ('it did seem to them after all that they had won a great victory'), explore how Orwell presents the difference between reality and propaganda in Animal Farm. Write about: how Orwell presents this difference in the extract, and how Orwell presents it in the novel as a whole.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. The windmill — years of backbreaking labour — has been destroyed, yet Napoleon declares 'a great victory.' The 'Order of the Green Banner, which he had conferred upon himself' is darkly comic — Napoleon awards himself for a battle he directed 'from the rear.' 'In the general rejoicings the unfortunate affair of the banknotes was forgotten' shows how celebrations are used to distract from failures. The pattern across the novel: every disaster is reframed as success (windmill destroyed by storm = Snowball's sabotage; forged banknotes = a lesson learned). Context: Stalin reframed the devastating German invasion as the 'Great Patriotic War.'
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Orwell use humour and irony to criticise Napoleon's leadership in Animal Farm?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (11-12) Critical, exploratory response. Orwell's satire works on multiple levels. The image of Napoleon 'wearing an old bowler hat of Mr. Jones's' and galloping drunkenly round the yard is comic but devastating — it visually represents the pigs becoming the humans they overthrew. 'Lord of the swill-bucket' deflates Napoleon's grandeur with bathos. The Fifth Commandment being changed to 'No animal shall drink alcohol to excess' is ironic because the pigs define 'excess' to suit themselves. The hens crediting Napoleon for their egg production is absurd comedy that exposes how cults of personality function. Orwell uses humour to make his political critique accessible — the reader laughs, then realises the horror beneath.

practice_questions.text: How does Orwell use the changing of the commandments throughout Animal Farm to present the corruption of the revolution?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (11-12) Critical, exploratory response. The commandments function as a barometer of corruption. Each change is small enough to go unnoticed: 'with sheets' (Ch.6), 'to excess' (Ch.8), 'without cause' (Ch.7). This gradual erosion mirrors how totalitarian regimes dismantle rights incrementally. The animals' inability to remember the originals highlights Orwell's warning about the importance of literacy and education. Clover checks the wall but cannot be certain it has changed. By Chapter Ten, all commandments are replaced by a single paradox: 'All animals are equal but some animals are more equal than others.' The revolution's foundational principles have been completely inverted. Context: parallels Stalin's systematic dismantling of Marxist principles while claiming to uphold them.

Chapter Nine: The Decline of Animal Farm

By Chapter Nine, life on Animal Farm has deteriorated drastically. Rations are reduced for all animals except the pigs and dogs — Orwell notes this through the understatement that ‘for the time being, certainly, it had been found necessary to make a readjustment of rations.’ The word ‘readjustment’ is a euphemism for a cut. Squealer reels off statistics to prove that food production has actually increased — but the animals are hungrier than ever.

The pigs, meanwhile, enjoy increasing privileges: a separate school for their piglets, beer rations (half a gallon for Napoleon, served in the Crown Derby soup tureen), and the right to walk on their hind legs within the farmhouse. Animal Farm is proclaimed a ‘Republic’ with Napoleon as its unanimously elected President — the only candidate. Orwell’s irony is devastating: a republic with a single candidate is a dictatorship by another name.

Key Fact

Orwell uses understatement throughout Chapter Nine to mirror Squealer’s propaganda techniques. By presenting terrible events in mild, bureaucratic language, Orwell shows how totalitarian regimes minimise suffering through carefully chosen words. The reader sees through the understatement even when the animals cannot.

Boxer’s Collapse

Boxer has been working himself to destruction. His split hoof, sustained during the Battle of the Windmill, never fully heals, yet he continues labouring on the new windmill. His determination to see the windmill completed before his retirement age of twelve drives him to work even harder. One day, Boxer collapses while hauling a load of stone. He falls to the ground and cannot get up.

The other animals are distraught. Boxer himself remains optimistic: he tells Clover that he will recover and spend his retirement in the corner of the big pasture that was set aside for retired animals. Orwell creates pathos through Boxer’s innocent hope — the reader knows, through dramatic irony, that the pigs have no intention of honouring their promise of retirement.

The Knacker’s Van

Squealer announces that Napoleon has arranged for Boxer to be treated at the hospital in Willingdon. A van arrives to collect him. But it is Benjamin — the cynical donkey, who can read — who notices the lettering on the side of the van: ‘Alfred Simmonds, Horse Slaughterer and Glue Boiler, Willingdon.’ For the first time in the novel, Benjamin breaks his silence and cries out: ‘Fools! Fools! Do you not see what is written on the side of that van?’

The animals rush after the van, screaming for Boxer to get out. Clover shouts, ‘Boxer! Boxer! Get out! Get out quickly! They’re taking you to your death!’ Boxer tries to kick his way out but ‘his strength had left him’ — the animal who was once the most powerful on the farm is now too weak to save himself. The van drives away. Boxer is never seen again.

Key Fact

The knacker’s van is the novel’s most emotionally devastating moment. Boxer — who gave everything to the farm, who worked when sick and injured, whose mottos were ‘I will work harder’ and ‘Napoleon is always right’ — is literally sold for slaughter. The pigs trade his body for whisky money. This is the ultimate betrayal of the working class.

Squealer’s Final Deception

Three days later, Squealer addresses the animals. He claims that Boxer died peacefully in hospital, with Squealer at his side. The van, Squealer explains, had previously belonged to a knacker but had been bought by the veterinary surgeon, who had not yet painted over the old lettering. The animals are ‘enormously relieved’ by this explanation. Orwell’s narration is deliberately flat and understated, forcing the reader to feel the outrage that the animals cannot.

Boxer represents the proletariat — the loyal, hardworking masses who pour their labour into building the state. His death at the knacker’s represents the totalitarian betrayal of workers: they are used, exploited, and discarded when they are no longer productive. In the Soviet Union, workers like the Stakhanovites were praised as heroes but received few real benefits. Those who became too old or sick to work were abandoned by the state they had served.

Orwell’s message is clear: totalitarian leaders view workers as resources, not people. The pigs’ use of the money from Boxer’s sale to buy whisky is the final, sickening proof — Boxer’s life is worth nothing more than a case of alcohol.

Benjamin’s Role

Benjamin’s reaction to the van is significant because he has spent the entire novel refusing to engage with the politics of the farm. His cynical motto — ‘Donkeys live a long time. None of you has ever seen a dead donkey’ — suggests he always knew the revolution would fail. But he never used his intelligence or literacy to warn the others. Only when his closest friend is about to die does he finally speak up — and by then it is too late.

Through Benjamin, Orwell warns that political apathy is as dangerous as active oppression. Benjamin could read, could think critically, and could see through the pigs’ lies — but he chose not to act. He represents the educated cynics who observe injustice but do nothing, believing change is impossible. Orwell suggests that their silence enables tyranny. Benjamin’s anguished cry of ‘Fools! Fools!’ is ultimately directed at himself as much as the other animals.

practice_questions.text: Read the following quotation: 'for the time being, certainly, it had been found necessary to make a readjustment of rations.' How does Orwell use language to present the pigs' manipulation in this quotation?
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis. E.g. 'Readjustment' is a euphemism for 'reduction' — Squealer uses bureaucratic language to disguise suffering. 'For the time being' implies the cut is temporary, when it is clearly permanent. 'Had been found necessary' uses passive voice to avoid attributing the decision to anyone — nobody is responsible. The phrase 'certainly' adds false confidence, as though the decision is beyond question. Orwell uses this understated language to mirror totalitarian propaganda: making terrible decisions sound reasonable.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comments. E.g. The pigs are reducing food but using nice words to make it sound better.

practice_questions.text: Starting with the extract describing Boxer being taken away in the van, explore how Orwell presents the theme of betrayal in Animal Farm. Write about: how Orwell presents betrayal in this extract, and how Orwell presents betrayal in the novel as a whole.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive, detailed analysis. The lettering on the van — 'Horse Slaughterer and Glue Boiler' — is blunt and brutal, contrasting with Squealer's gentle lie about a 'hospital.' Boxer's inability to kick his way out ('his strength had left him') is heartbreaking: the strongest animal on the farm is now powerless. Clover's desperate scream creates pathos. This betrayal is the culmination of a pattern: the pigs have been betraying the animals since they took the milk in Chapter Two. Each betrayal is larger: milk → beds → executions → Boxer's murder. The revolution itself is a betrayal of Old Major's vision. Context: parallels the Soviet state's abandonment of workers who had built the nation.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with textual references.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How far does Orwell present Boxer as a sympathetic character in Animal Farm? Write about: what Boxer says and does, and how far Orwell presents Boxer as a sympathetic character.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26–30 marks + up to 4 spelling/grammar)Critical, exploratory response. Boxer is Orwell's most sympathetic creation. His physical strength ('equal to that of all the rest of the animals put together'), his selfless mottos ('I will work harder'), and his genuine belief in the revolution's ideals make him deeply admirable. His collapse while hauling stone and his innocent hope for retirement create powerful pathos. The scene at the knacker's van is devastating precisely because the reader has grown to love Boxer. HOWEVER — Orwell also invites criticism. Boxer's second motto, 'Napoleon is always right', represents the danger of blind loyalty. His refusal to think critically enables the pigs' tyranny. When Boxer accepts Squealer's lies about Snowball despite his own memories, he surrenders his moral agency. Orwell creates sympathy to make a political point: the exploitation of loyal, uncritical workers is one of totalitarianism's greatest crimes. Context: Boxer parallels Stakhanovite workers — praised as heroes but ultimately expendable.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful, developed response. Top band (16-20): Clear, explained response. Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained response. Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported response. Lower band (1-5): Simple response.
spelling/grammar: 4 marks for consistent accuracy in spelling, punctuation, and grammar with effective use of vocabulary.

practice_questions.text: Starting with the extract where Squealer explains that Boxer died peacefully in hospital, explore how Orwell presents lies and deception in Animal Farm. Write about: how Orwell presents deception in this extract, and how Orwell presents deception in the novel as a whole.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. Squealer's claim that the van 'had previously belonged to a knacker' and the vet 'had not yet painted over the old name' is an absurdly transparent lie — yet the animals are 'enormously relieved.' Their relief reveals how desperate they are to believe the lie rather than face the truth. This mirrors a pattern: the animals have been accepting increasingly outrageous lies throughout the novel (Snowball as traitor, changed commandments). Orwell's flat, understated narration forces the reader to supply the outrage. Context: in the USSR, citizens were fed constant lies about food production, political prisoners, and working conditions, and many chose to believe rather than risk dissent.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Orwell use the character of Benjamin to explore ideas about political responsibility in Animal Farm?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (11-12) Critical, exploratory response. Benjamin is one of the most complex characters in Animal Farm. He represents the educated cynic who sees through propaganda but refuses to act. His cynicism ('Donkeys live a long time') masks a deeper despair about the possibility of change. Unlike Boxer, Benjamin can read and think critically — but he wastes these gifts through inaction. His scream of 'Fools! Fools!' at the knacker's van is the novel's most tragic moment of self-awareness: he finally acts, but too late. Orwell suggests that Benjamin's silence was as harmful as Squealer's lies — both enable tyranny, one actively and one passively. This is a warning to the reader: political apathy has consequences.
Upper band (9-10) Thoughtful response.
Top band (7-8): Clear, relevant response.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple response.

practice_questions.text: How does Orwell use the pigs' increasing privileges in Chapter Nine to develop the theme of inequality in Animal Farm?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (11-12) Critical, exploratory response. Chapter Nine catalogues the pigs' privileges with devastating precision: beer rations, separate schooling for piglets, reduced working hours. Napoleon drinks from the 'Crown Derby soup tureen' — an object associated with human luxury. The 'Republic' with a single candidate is Orwell's most pointed political satire. Each privilege directly contradicts a principle of Animalism: equality is replaced by hierarchy, communal living by class separation. The 'spontaneous demonstrations' are involuntary celebrations of their own oppression. Orwell shows that revolution does not eliminate inequality — it merely replaces one elite with another. Context: Stalin lived in luxury while millions of Soviet citizens starved during the 1930s famines.
Upper band (9-10) Thoughtful response.
Top band (7-8): Clear response.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple response.

Chapter Ten: The Passage of Time

Chapter Ten opens with a time-jump. Years have passed. Many of the original animals who took part in the Rebellion are dead. Boxer, Snowball, Old Major, and Jones are all gone. Only Clover, Benjamin, Moses the raven, and ‘a number of the pigs’ remain from the revolutionary generation. The farm has new animals who have never known anything other than Napoleon’s rule — they accept it as normal.

Orwell’s description of Napoleon and Squealer is pointed: both have grown enormously fat. Napoleon weighs ‘twenty-four stone’ and Squealer is so obese his eyes are barely visible. Their physical transformation mirrors their moral corruption — they have literally fattened themselves on the labour of others. The farm now ‘possessed’ three horses, a cart, and a plough — the word ‘possessed’ is significant because it implies the animals are property once more.

Key Fact

The time-jump is a deliberate structural choice. Orwell skips forward to show the long-term consequences of the revolution’s failure. The new generation of animals, who never knew Old Major’s vision, accept tyranny as normal — Orwell warns that without historical memory, oppression becomes invisible.

The Final Commandment

The Seven Commandments have been progressively altered throughout the novel. Now, in Chapter Ten, they are replaced entirely by a single commandment painted on the barn wall in enormous letters:

‘ALL ANIMALS ARE EQUAL BUT SOME ANIMALS ARE MORE EQUAL THAN OTHERS.’

This paradox is the novel’s most famous line. It is a logical impossibility — if some are ‘more equal,’ then none are truly equal. Orwell uses this contradiction to expose the fundamental lie at the heart of the pigs’ rule: they have claimed to uphold equality while systematically destroying it. The commandment also serves as Orwell’s critique of the Soviet Union, where the Communist Party’s promise of a classless society became a justification for a new ruling elite.

Original: ‘No animal shall sleep in a bed.’ Changed to: ‘No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets.’ (Ch.6)

Original: ‘No animal shall kill any other animal.’ Changed to: ‘No animal shall kill any other animal without cause.’ (Ch.7)

Original: ‘No animal shall drink alcohol.’ Changed to: ‘No animal shall drink alcohol to excess.’ (Ch.8)

Final replacement: ‘All animals are equal but some animals are more equal than others.’ (Ch.10) — All seven commandments are erased and replaced with this single paradox, completing the revolution’s betrayal.

The Pigs Become Humans

The pigs now walk on their hind legs. Napoleon emerges from the farmhouse carrying a whip — the very symbol of Jones’s human oppression that the animals rebelled against in Chapter Two. The sheep, retrained by Squealer, now bleat ‘Four legs good, two legs better’ — a complete inversion of the original slogan. The animals who remember the old days are too few, too old, and too afraid to object.

In the novel’s climactic scene, Napoleon invites neighbouring farmers — Mr Pilkington of Foxwood — to dinner at the farmhouse. The animals peer through the window and watch pigs and humans playing cards, drinking, and laughing together. Pilkington congratulates Napoleon on running a farm where ‘the lower animals did more work and received less food than any animals in the county.’ Napoleon announces that ‘Animal Farm’ will henceforth be known simply as ‘the Manor Farm’ — its original name under Jones.

Key Fact

The renaming of Animal Farm back to Manor Farm is the final symbol of the revolution’s complete failure. The word ‘revolution’ literally means ‘a complete turn’ — the farm has turned all the way back to where it started.

The Final Image

The novel ends with one of the most powerful closing lines in English literature:

‘The creatures outside looked from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again; but already it was impossible to say which was which.’

This image is devastating. The pigs have become physically and morally indistinguishable from the humans they overthrew. Orwell’s allegory reaches its conclusion: the revolution has produced a new class of oppressors who are identical to the old ones. The ‘creatures outside’ — the ordinary animals, the working class — are left staring through a window at a world of power and privilege from which they are permanently excluded.

Pessimistic: The revolution has achieved nothing. The animals are worse off than under Jones. There is no hope of further rebellion — the new generation accepts tyranny as normal. Power always corrupts.

Realistic: Orwell was a democratic socialist who believed in equality but saw how revolutionary ideals were betrayed in practice. The ending reflects his view that Stalinism specifically — not socialism itself — had failed.

Optimistic (arguably): The quarrel between pigs and humans at the card game suggests that the alliance between the ruling classes is unstable. The animals are still watching through the window — perhaps awareness is the first step toward future resistance.

Orwell’s Moral

Orwell described Animal Farm as a fable. Like all fables, it carries a moral. Orwell’s warnings are multiple: that revolutions are vulnerable to hijacking by those who seek personal power; that propaganda and the manipulation of language can make people accept any injustice; that political apathy enables tyranny; and that without education, literacy, and the freedom to question authority, ordinary people will always be exploited by those who rule them.
